name: Prefab veneers (Snap-On Smile)

lead: Prefab veneers are removable shells worn over the teeth to change how the smile looks: whiter colour, more even shape and masked gaps, visible the moment they go on. They are not bonded and can be taken out, which separates them from dentist-made veneers.
A preformed cover fits over the existing teeth and is held in place by fit rather than bonding. Little published research or encyclopedic coverage addresses removable clip-on veneers specifically.

paras: People buy a kit online, fit the covers over their teeth, and wear them for photos, events or work, taking them out for eating and cleaning. Some use them as a preview before deciding on bonded veneers or other dental work.
No safety or effectiveness studies on removable veneers were found. Information on bonded veneers does not directly apply to them.

angle.text: Users clip on prefab veneers like Snap-On Smile to change the colour, shape or spacing of their front teeth without dentistry, and the change is visible while worn. They are removable, unlike bonded veneers. No research on these removable covers was found.

lead: Prefab or snap-on veneers are removable cosmetic covers that fit over the front teeth to change their apparent colour, shape and spacing without drilling or bonding. People use them as an immediate way to get a whiter, more even-looking smile, covering stains, chips, gaps or missing teeth, and can take them out again.[1]

They differ from bonded veneers, which are thin porcelain or composite coverings attached to the tooth, usually for discolouration, enamel defects, fractures and shape changes.[2] The best-documented branded version, Snap-On Smile, is a custom arch made by a dental laboratory in a thin resin from a dentist's impression, fitted over three visits, and described by its maker as removable and reversible.[1]

Published literature consists mainly of dentist-written clinical descriptions and case reports, including use in amelogenesis imperfecta, as an interim restoration before porcelain veneers, and as a non-invasive option for older patients; no controlled trials were found.[3][4][5]
infobox: No, removable (Snap-On Smile says no adhesives needed)[1]
Dentist impression, laboratory-made, three visits (Snap-On Smile)[1]

paras: Dental veneers in the clinical sense are made mainly of composite or dental porcelain and bonded to the tooth; porcelain versions are made indirectly in a laboratory.[2] Removable snap-on products are a separate category held in place by fit rather than by bonding.[1]

The Snap-On Smile system is described by its maker as a custom removable arch that covers stains, chips, gaps and missing teeth. A dentist takes an impression, typically without injections, drilling or removal of tooth structure, a dental laboratory fabricates the arch and the dentist fits it at the final visit. It is marketed as an affordable, non-invasive alternative to veneers, implants or dentures, usable temporarily or long term, and the maker states that eating and drinking are possible while wearing it, with sticky foods avoided.[1]

A 2006 article in Dentistry Today describes clinical applications and two case studies of Snap-On Smile.[5][6] A 2015 case in the Journal of the Tennessee Dental Association used it for a preteen with amelogenesis imperfecta, a hereditary enamel disorder with discoloured, sensitive teeth, to improve appearance without altering the developing dentition.[4]

A 2020 article in the Journal of Esthetic and Restorative Dentistry describes snap-on provisional restorations for veneer cases, which patients can clean easily so soft tissues are healthier before final cementation; the authors describe it as an effective provisionalization option accepted by patients.[3] A 2016 case report describes a Snap-On-Smile overdenture for a 78-year-old with osteonecrosis of the jaw, restoring speech, function and esthetics.[7] A 2013 trade article presents it as a convenient option for older patients.[8]
No controlled studies found. Published work consists of clinical technique descriptions and case reports, mainly from dentists.[3][4][5][7]
